standard.title: Apostrophes for contraction and possession
standard.description: understand that apostrophes signal missing letters in contractions, and apostrophes show possession
standard.prior_knowledge: Students recognise how capital letters and commas are used in titles and lists (AC9E2LA10). They have not yet examined apostrophes — either for contraction or for possession.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand that apostrophes signal missing letters in contractions and show possession (singular and plural).

nodes.label: Apostrophes in contractions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can form and interpret contractions using apostrophes to signal the missing letter(s).
nodes.minimum_width: Form at least three contractions correctly using apostrophes (e.g. do not → don't, will not → won't) and explain what the apostrophe signals.
nodes.typical_width: Use apostrophes to create contractions from common word pairs; understand that the apostrophe marks where letters have been omitted; recognise contractions in reading.
wider: Investigate why 'won't' doesn't follow the expected pattern for 'will not', and explore other irregular contractions
Discuss when contractions are appropriate versus when full forms are preferred — comparing informal and formal text contexts

response_modes.reason: Apostrophe use in contractions is a precision convention — students understand the concept quickly but errors (especially 'wont', 'dont') persist in writing without targeted practice. Fluency requires repeated application.

success_criteria: Student correctly places the apostrophe in a contraction at the point of omission
Student can identify what letters have been removed to form the contraction

nodes.label: Apostrophes for possession
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use apostrophes to show singular and plural possession.
nodes.minimum_width: Correctly form singular possession (e.g. my friend's book) and at least one plural possession (e.g. the bees' hive) using an apostrophe.
nodes.typical_width: Use apostrophes to show singular possession (noun + 's) and plural possession (plural noun + ') in a range of contexts; recognise and correct possession apostrophe errors.
wider: Explore the irregular plural possessive (e.g. children's, men's) — where the apostrophe follows different rules — and discuss why
Compare possession expressed with an apostrophe versus a phrase (the book belonging to my friend) and discuss when each is preferred

response_modes.reason: Possessive apostrophe errors (especially plural possession and confusion with plural 's') are highly persistent in student writing. This is a mechanical precision skill where practice — not additional contexts — is the remedy.

The singular/plural possession distinction (friend's vs friends') is a genuine point where the rule changes. Seeing multiple examples of both types — and irregular cases — helps students develop reliable discrimination rather than guessing.

success_criteria: Student correctly places the apostrophe for singular possession
Student correctly places the apostrophe for at least one regular plural possession
